author and date: Moses, by long Jewish and Christian tradition (Jn 5:46); written in the wilderness, c. 1446–1406 BC on the early Exodus date. Some hold later editorial touches (e.g. the place names in 14:14).
setting and audience: Israel at Sinai and on the way to Canaan, who needed to know where they came from and why God had chosen them.
structure: 1–11 the beginnings: creation, fall, flood, Babel. 12–50 the fathers: Abraham (12–25), Isaac and Jacob (25–36), Joseph (37–50).
message: God creates a good world, man falls, and God promises a Seed who will crush the serpent (3:15) and bless all nations through Abraham (12:3; 15; 17). The Seed is Christ (Gal 3:16).

author and date: Moses. The date of the Exodus is debated: c. 1446 BC (an early date, from 1 Ki 6:1) or c. 1260 BC (a late date). [INTRA-REFORMED DEBATE]
setting and audience: Israel, a people enslaved in Egypt, then redeemed and formed into a nation at Sinai.
structure: 1–15 deliverance from Egypt (the plagues, the Passover, the Red Sea). 16–18 the wilderness. 19–24 the covenant at Sinai and the Ten Commandments. 25–40 the tabernacle and its worship.
message: God redeems first and then gives the law, so obedience answers grace. The Passover lamb points to Christ (1 Cor 5:7) and the tabernacle to God dwelling among his people (Jn 1:14).

author and date: Moses, at Sinai, in the year after the Exodus.
setting and audience: The priests and people of Israel, taught how a sinful people can live near a holy God.
structure: 1–7 the offerings. 8–10 the priesthood. 11–15 clean and unclean. 16 the Day of Atonement. 17–27 the call to holiness: “you shall be holy, for I am holy” (19:2).
message: Sin needs atonement by blood, and only holiness may approach God. Hebrews 7–10 shows Christ as the final priest and the one sacrifice.

author and date: Moses; the events cover about 38 years in the wilderness after Sinai (c. 1445–1406 BC on the early date).
setting and audience: Israel travelling from Sinai towards Canaan, and the new generation that would enter it.
structure: 1–10 ready to leave Sinai (the census, the camp). 11–25 complaint, the unbelief at Kadesh (13–14), judgement and wandering. 26–36 the new generation on the plains of Moab.
message: Unbelief is judged, yet God keeps his promise to the next generation. The bronze serpent lifted up points to the cross (Jn 3:14), and Paul takes the wilderness as a warning to the church (1 Cor 10:1–12).

author and date: Moses, in the last weeks of his life, with the account of his death added at the end.
setting and audience: The new generation on the plains of Moab, about to cross the Jordan.
structure: 1–4 what God has done. 5–26 the law explained (the Ten Commandments in 5, the Shema in 6:4–5). 27–30 the covenant, with blessings and curses. 31–34 Joshua succeeds Moses; Moses’ song and death.
message: The form is that of an ancient treaty between a king and his people. The call is to love the LORD with all one’s heart. God promises a prophet like Moses (18:15), whom the New Testament identifies as Christ (Acts 3:22). Jesus answered Satan from this book.

author and date: Tradition names Joshua; later hands added some details (24:29–33). The conquest is dated c. 1406–1390 BC (early) or in the 13th century BC (late).
setting and audience: Israel crossing the Jordan and receiving the land promised to Abraham.
structure: 1–5 entering the land. 6–12 the conquest (Jericho, Ai, the south, the north). 13–21 the land divided among the tribes. 22–24 the farewell and renewal of the covenant at Shechem.
message: God gives what he promised. Joshua’s name is “Jesus” in the Greek, and the rest in the land points to the greater rest in Christ (Heb 4:8–9).

author and date: The author is not named (Jewish tradition says Samuel). It covers about 350 years, c. 1380–1050 BC, and was written after the kingdom began (“in those days there was no king”).
setting and audience: Israel after Joshua’s death, settled in the land and often unfaithful.
structure: 1–2 failure to finish the conquest. 3–16 the cycle of sin, oppression, cry for help and a deliverer, through twelve judges (Othniel, Deborah, Gideon, Samson). 17–21 two stories showing how far the people had fallen.
message: The people repeat their sin and God raises up saviours, who are flawed. The book ends by asking for a king who will do right, which looks ahead to David and to Christ.

author and date: The author is not named. It is set in the time of the judges and was written in the days of the monarchy, since it ends with David’s line.
setting and audience: Naomi’s family in Moab and Bethlehem, a story told for a people who knew the covenant.
structure: 1 Naomi and Ruth return to Bethlehem. 2–3 Ruth and Boaz. 4 Boaz redeems and marries Ruth, and the line of David is traced.
message: The kinsman-redeemer buys back what was lost. A Moabite woman enters the line of David and of Christ (Mt 1:5), which shows God’s grace reaching beyond Israel.

author and date: The author is not named (the prophets Samuel, Nathan and Gad are suggested by 1 Chr 29:29). It covers c. 1100–1010 BC.
setting and audience: Israel at the end of the judges, asking for a king.
structure: 1–7 Eli and Samuel. 8–15 Saul, the people’s choice, and his rejection. 16–31 David’s anointing, his rise and Saul’s fall.
message: The people’s king fails, and God chooses a king after his own heart (13:14). Hannah’s song (2:1–10) already speaks of the LORD’s “anointed” (the Messiah).

author and date: The author is not named; the book was a single work with 1 Samuel. It covers David’s reign, c. 1010–970 BC.
setting and audience: Israel under David, from Hebron to Jerusalem.
structure: 1–10 David becomes king of all Israel. 11–20 his sin with Bathsheba and its consequences. 21–24 appendices, including David’s last words and the census.
message: In chapter 7 God promises David a house and a throne for ever. Christ is the Son of David who fulfils it (Lk 1:32–33), and David’s sin shows that he is not the final king.

author and date: The author is not named (Jewish tradition says Jeremiah). It covers c. 970–853 BC and was put together during the exile, after 561 BC (2 Ki 25:27).
setting and audience: Judah and Israel, first united under Solomon and then divided.
structure: 1–11 Solomon: his wisdom, the temple, his fall into idolatry. 12–22 the kingdom splits, and Elijah confronts Ahab and Baal.
message: The temple is built, and the kings are weighed against the covenant of Moses. The question is faithfulness to the LORD alone.

author and date: As 1 Kings; it covers c. 853–586 BC, from Elisha to the fall of Jerusalem.
setting and audience: The two kingdoms until their end, told for the exiles in Babylon.
structure: 1–17 Israel and Judah side by side, to the fall of Samaria (722 BC). 18–25 Judah alone: Hezekiah, Josiah, the fall of Jerusalem (586 BC), the exile.
message: The covenant curses of Deuteronomy come true. The book ends with a note of hope: Jehoiachin, of David’s line, is released from prison (25:27–30).

author and date: The author is not named (Jewish tradition says Ezra). Written after the exile, c. 450–400 BC.
setting and audience: The community returned from Babylon, who needed to know who they were.
structure: 1–9 the genealogies from Adam to the returned exiles. 10–29 the reign of David and his preparation for the temple.
message: It stresses the line of David and the right worship of God. It tells the returned people that the promises to David still stand.

author and date: As 1 Chronicles. Written after the exile, c. 450–400 BC.
setting and audience: The returned community in Judah.
structure: 1–9 Solomon and the building of the temple. 10–36 the kings of Judah, to the exile and the decree of Cyrus (36:22–23).
message: “If my people… humble themselves and pray and seek my face… I will hear” (7:14). Repentance brings restoration, and the book ends on a call to return.

author and date: Tradition names Ezra the scribe, who is also the central figure from chapter 7. It covers 538–c. 458 BC.
setting and audience: The Jews returning from exile under the Persian kings.
structure: 1–6 the return under Zerubbabel and the rebuilding of the temple (finished 516 BC). 7–10 Ezra comes, teaches the Law and leads the people in reform.
message: God keeps his word about the return (Jer 29:10), working through pagan kings. The Law and right worship must be re-established.

author and date: Nehemiah, the king’s cupbearer, who wrote his own memoirs. It covers c. 445–425 BC.
setting and audience: Jerusalem, still in ruins, under Persian rule.
structure: 1–7 Nehemiah rebuilds the wall in 52 days. 8–10 Ezra reads the Law, and the people renew the covenant. 11–13 resettlement and reforms.
message: Prayer and work go together, and renewal comes through the public reading of God’s Word (ch. 8).

author and date: The author is not named. It is set in the reign of Xerxes (Ahasuerus), c. 483–473 BC.
setting and audience: Jews living in the Persian empire after the exile.
structure: 1–2 Esther becomes queen. 3–7 Haman’s plot against the Jews and Esther’s courage. 8–10 deliverance and the feast of Purim.
message: God is not named, yet his providence rules everything, and his people are preserved (4:14), including the line of the Messiah.

author and date: The author is not named, and the date of writing is uncertain. The story is set in the age of the patriarchs.
setting and audience: Job, a righteous man, suffers, and his friends misjudge him.
structure: 1–2 prologue: Satan’s challenge and Job’s afflictions. 3–37 the debates between Job, his three friends and Elihu. 38–42 the LORD answers from the whirlwind, and Job is restored.
message: Suffering is not always punishment. God is sovereign and wise beyond our understanding, and Job says, “I know that my Redeemer lives” (19:25).

author and date: David wrote about half (73 psalms are headed with his name), with Asaph, the sons of Korah, Solomon, Moses (90) and others. The collection grew from c. 1400 to c. 450 BC.
setting and audience: Israel’s hymnbook for worship, public and private.
structure: Five books: 1–41, 42–72, 73–89, 90–106, 107–150, each ending with a doxology. The kinds of psalm include praise, lament, royal, wisdom and thanksgiving.
message: Christ is found in the Psalms (Lk 24:44): the King (2, 110), the sufferer (22), the Shepherd (23). The Reformed churches have long sung them in worship.

author and date: Solomon is the chief author (1:1), with sayings of the wise, of Agur and Lemuel, and a section copied by Hezekiah’s men (25:1). c. 950–700 BC.
setting and audience: Israel’s young people, taught how to live in God’s world.
structure: 1–9 a father’s speeches on wisdom and folly. 10–22:16 Solomon’s sayings. 22:17–24 the sayings of the wise. 25–29 Hezekiah’s collection. 30–31 Agur, Lemuel and the wife of noble character.
message: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (1:7). The wisdom of God is personified, and Christ is “the wisdom of God” (1 Cor 1:24).

author and date: “The Preacher,” traditionally Solomon (c. 935 BC). Some date it later. [INTRA-REFORMED DEBATE]
setting and audience: Anyone who asks what life under the sun is worth.
structure: 1–2 everything is “vanity.” 3–11 reflections on time, work, wealth, justice and death. 12 the conclusion: fear God and keep his commandments.
message: Life without God is empty and cannot be controlled. Enjoy God’s gifts and fear him, and look to the judge of all.

author and date: Solomon (1:1), c. 950 BC.
setting and audience: Israel, a love poem for a people whose God uses marriage as an image of himself.
structure: Poems of the bride and bridegroom, in courtship, wedding and marriage.
message: It praises the gift of married love (Gen 2:24). Christians have also read it as a picture of Christ and his church (Eph 5:32). The balance between the literal and the typological sense is debated. [INTRA-REFORMED DEBATE]

author and date: Isaiah son of Amoz, who prophesied in Jerusalem under Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, c. 740–680 BC. Critical scholars divide the book between two or three authors; the Reformed tradition holds that it is one.
setting and audience: Judah threatened by Assyria, with words reaching to the exile and beyond.
structure: 1–39 judgement on Judah and the nations, and the promise of Immanuel (7:14; 9:6). 40–55 comfort for the exiles, and the Servant of the LORD (ch. 53). 56–66 the new heavens and the new earth.
message: The most quoted Old Testament book in the New. The holy God judges, then saves through the suffering Servant, who is Jesus (Acts 8:32–35).

author and date: Jeremiah, priest and prophet, who spoke c. 627–580 BC. Baruch was his scribe.
setting and audience: Judah in its last decades, falling to Babylon in 586 BC.
structure: 1 the call. 2–25 judgement on Judah. 26–45 conflict with kings and the Book of Consolation (30–33). 46–51 the nations. 52 the fall of Jerusalem.
message: The people broke the covenant, and God promises a new covenant, written on the heart (31:31–34), which Hebrews 8 says Christ has made.

author and date: Tradition names Jeremiah; written after 586 BC.
setting and audience: Survivors mourning the destruction of Jerusalem.
structure: Five poems, four of them acrostics (each verse or group of verses begins with a letter of the Hebrew alphabet).
message: Grief is held within faith: “his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning” (3:22–23).

author and date: Ezekiel, a priest taken to Babylon in 597 BC, who prophesied 593–571 BC.
setting and audience: The exiles by the river Chebar.
structure: 1–24 the glory leaves and Jerusalem is condemned. 25–32 the nations. 33–48 restoration: the dry bones (37), the new covenant, the new temple (40–48).
message: The LORD’s glory is not tied to the temple. God promises a new heart and his Spirit (36:26–27). The meaning of the temple vision is debated. [INTRA-REFORMED DEBATE]

author and date: Daniel, taken to Babylon in 605 BC and serving until the Persian period (c. 530). Critical scholars date the book to the 160s BC; the Reformed tradition holds the 6th century.
setting and audience: Jews in exile, serving foreign kings.
structure: 1–6 stories of faithfulness (the fiery furnace, the lions’ den). 7–12 visions: four kingdoms, the Son of Man (7:13–14), the seventy weeks (9).
message: The Most High rules all kingdoms and gives an everlasting kingdom to the Son of Man, a title Jesus takes for himself. The seventy weeks are read in several ways. [INTRA-REFORMED DEBATE]

author and date: Hosea, who prophesied in the northern kingdom, c. 755–715 BC.
setting and audience: Israel, prosperous and idolatrous before Assyria took it.
structure: 1–3 Hosea’s marriage to unfaithful Gomer as a picture of God and Israel. 4–14 charges, judgement and the promise of return.
message: The LORD’s steadfast covenant love (hesed) persists despite his people’s unfaithfulness. “Out of Egypt I called my son” (11:1) is applied to Christ in Matthew 2:15.

author and date: Joel; the date is uncertain (9th century or after the exile). [INTRA-REFORMED DEBATE]
setting and audience: Judah after a plague of locusts.
structure: 1:1–2:17 the locusts and the call to repent. 2:18–3:21 the LORD’s answer, the promise of the Spirit and the day of the LORD.
message: “I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh” (2:28) was fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2:16–21).

author and date: Amos, a shepherd of Tekoa, who prophesied c. 760 BC in the north.
setting and audience: Israel in prosperity under Jeroboam II, with injustice at home.
structure: 1–2 judgement on the nations and on Israel. 3–6 charges against Israel’s wealth and false worship. 7–9 five visions and the promise to raise David’s fallen tent (9:11).
message: God demands justice (5:24). James quotes 9:11–12 at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:16–17) for the inclusion of the Gentiles.

author and date: Obadiah; the date is debated (probably after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC).
setting and audience: Edom, Judah’s neighbour, who gloated over Jerusalem’s fall.
structure: 1–9 Edom’s fall. 10–14 the reason: violence against Jacob. 15–21 the day of the LORD and the kingdom of the LORD.
message: Pride before God brings judgement, and “the kingdom shall be the LORD’s” (v. 21).

author and date: Jonah son of Amittai (2 Ki 14:25), c. 780–750 BC.
setting and audience: Nineveh, capital of Assyria, Israel’s enemy.
structure: 1 Jonah flees. 2 his prayer in the fish. 3 Nineveh repents. 4 Jonah’s anger and the LORD’s question.
message: God’s mercy reaches foreign enemies, and the book ends on his compassion. Jesus calls his own resurrection “the sign of Jonah” (Mt 12:39–41).

author and date: Micah of Moresheth, c. 740–700 BC, a contemporary of Isaiah.
setting and audience: Judah and Israel under Assyrian threat.
structure: 1–3 judgement. 4–5 hope, and the ruler to be born in Bethlehem (5:2). 6–7 the LORD’s case against his people, “do justice, love kindness, walk humbly” (6:8), and God’s pardon (7:18–20).
message: The Christ is born in Bethlehem (Mt 2:6), and God casts our sins into the sea.

author and date: Nahum, c. 663–612 BC, before the fall of Nineveh (612 BC).
setting and audience: Assyria and Nineveh, which had once repented under Jonah.
structure: 1 the LORD is good and a refuge, yet avenges. 2–3 the fall of Nineveh.
message: God judges violence and cruelty, and he cares for those who trust him (1:7).

author and date: Habakkuk, c. 609–598 BC, before the Babylonian invasion.
setting and audience: Judah, facing violence from within and Babylon from without.
structure: 1:1–2:5 the prophet’s two questions and the LORD’s answers. 2:6–20 five woes. 3 a prayer and song of faith.
message: “The righteous shall live by his faith” (2:4), a text that stands behind Romans 1:17, Galatians 3:11 and Hebrews 10:38.

author and date: Zephaniah, in the reign of Josiah (640–609 BC).
setting and audience: Judah before Josiah’s reform and the fall of Jerusalem.
structure: 1:1–2:3 the day of the LORD against Judah. 2:4–3:7 the nations and Jerusalem. 3:8–20 the remnant and the restoration.
message: The day of the LORD is a day of wrath, yet God will gather a humble remnant and “rejoice over you with gladness” (3:17).

author and date: Haggai, in 520 BC (four messages in four months).
setting and audience: The returned exiles who had put their own houses before the temple.
structure: 1 the call to build the house of the LORD. 2 the glory of the later house, and Zerubbabel as the LORD’s signet.
message: God’s presence is the true glory of the temple. The “desire of the nations” comes to fill it (2:7).

author and date: Zechariah, from 520 BC to about 480 BC. Critical scholars divide chapters 9–14 from 1–8; conservatives hold the book to be one.
setting and audience: The returned community rebuilding the temple.
structure: 1–6 eight night visions. 7–8 the question of fasting. 9–14 two oracles: the coming king, the shepherd struck, the day of the LORD.
message: The king comes “humble and mounted on a donkey” (9:9, Mt 21:5), and “they will look on him whom they have pierced” (12:10, Jn 19:37).

author and date: Malachi, c. 460–430 BC, after the temple was rebuilt.
setting and audience: A discouraged community with careless worship.
structure: 1:2–4:3 six disputes: God’s love, polluted offerings, faithless priests and marriages, justice, tithes, and hard words against God. 4:4–6 the call to remember the law and the promise of Elijah.
message: The Lord will come to his temple (3:1). John the Baptist is the messenger who prepares the way (Mt 11:10–14), and the Old Testament ends looking forward.

author and date: Matthew, the apostle and former tax collector (by early church tradition), c. AD 50s–60s; many date it in the 60s to 80s.
setting and audience: Jewish Christians, to show that Jesus is the promised Messiah.
structure: 1–2 the birth and infancy. 3–4 baptism and temptation. 5–25 the ministry in five discourses (the Sermon on the Mount, 5–7; the mission, 10; the parables, 13; the church, 18; the end, 24–25). 26–28 the passion, the resurrection and the Great Commission.
message: Jesus is the Son of David and Son of Abraham, the king in whom the Old Testament is fulfilled (“that it might be fulfilled” recurs), and he commands that all nations be discipled (28:18–20).

author and date: John Mark, writing from Peter’s preaching (as Papias and the early church say), probably in Rome, c. AD 55–65. The last verses (16:9–20) are absent from the oldest manuscripts and are debated.
setting and audience: Gentile, probably Roman, Christians facing suffering.
structure: 1:1–8:26 the ministry in Galilee. 8:27–10:52 the way to the cross, with Peter’s confession in 8:29. 11–16 the last week, the passion and the resurrection.
message: Jesus is the Son of God, who came “to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many” (10:45). The book is short and moves fast.

author and date: Luke the physician, Paul’s companion, who also wrote Acts. Probably c. AD 60–62, before Acts.
setting and audience: Theophilus and other Gentile readers, for certainty about what they were taught (1:1–4).
structure: 1–2 the birth and infancy. 3:1–9:50 the ministry in Galilee. 9:51–19:27 the journey to Jerusalem. 19:28–24 the passion, the resurrection and the walk to Emmaus.
message: Jesus is the Saviour of all, including the poor, the outcast and the sinner (19:10). On the road to Emmaus he opens “all the Scriptures” to show that they speak of himself (24:27).

author and date: The apostle John, probably from Ephesus, c. AD 80–90 (some argue for an earlier date).
setting and audience: Believers and enquirers, “that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God” (20:31).
structure: 1:1–18 the Word became flesh. 1:19–12 the signs, with the “I am” sayings. 13–17 the upper room and the farewell. 18–21 the passion, the resurrection and the restoration of Peter.
message: Jesus is God the Son who became man. Whoever believes in him has life in his name. The Spirit will come (14–16).

author and date: Luke, c. AD 62, covering AD 30–62.
setting and audience: Theophilus, as the second volume to Luke’s Gospel.
structure: 1–7 Jerusalem. 8–12 Judea and Samaria. 13–28 to the ends of the earth: Paul’s journeys (13–21), his arrest and voyage to Rome (21–28). The council of Jerusalem is in 15.
message: The risen Christ builds his church by the Spirit and the Word (1:8). Salvation spreads from the Jews to the Gentiles.

author and date: Paul, from Corinth, c. AD 57.
setting and audience: The church at Rome, which Paul had not yet visited.
structure: 1:18–3:20 all are under sin. 3:21–5 justification by faith alone. 6–8 life in the Spirit and assurance (8:28–39). 9–11 God’s purpose for Israel. 12–16 the Christian life.
message: The gospel is the power of God for salvation, “the righteous shall live by faith” (1:16–17). This letter was the centre of the Reformation (sola fide).

author and date: Paul, from Ephesus, c. AD 55.
setting and audience: The church at Corinth, divided and disorderly.
structure: 1–4 divisions and the wisdom of the cross. 5–6 immorality and lawsuits. 7–10 marriage, idols and liberty. 11–14 worship, the Lord’s Supper and gifts. 15 the resurrection. 16 the collection.
message: The cross is God’s wisdom, the church is one body, and Christ’s resurrection guarantees ours (15).

author and date: Paul, from Macedonia, c. AD 56. Paul wrote other letters to Corinth that are lost.
setting and audience: The same church, after a painful visit.
structure: 1–7 the new covenant ministry and reconciliation. 8–9 the collection for Jerusalem. 10–13 Paul’s defence of his apostleship.
message: God’s power is made perfect in weakness (12:9). “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (5:19).

author and date: Paul, c. AD 48–49 (if the churches were in south Galatia) or in the mid-50s.
setting and audience: The churches of Galatia, which were turning to a gospel of works.
structure: 1–2 Paul’s gospel is from Christ, and the confrontation at Antioch. 3–4 justification by faith, as with Abraham. 5–6 freedom and the fruit of the Spirit.
message: “A person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ” (2:16). It is the other great book of the Reformation.

author and date: Paul, from prison in Rome, c. AD 60–62.
setting and audience: The churches of Asia Minor, probably a circular letter.
structure: 1–3 what God has done: chosen in Christ (1:4), saved by grace through faith (2:8–9), Jew and Gentile made one. 4–6 how to walk: unity, holiness, households and the armour of God.
message: God’s eternal plan is to unite all things in Christ, and the church is his body.

author and date: Paul, from prison, c. AD 60–62.
setting and audience: The church at Philippi, which had sent a gift.
structure: 1 Paul’s imprisonment and joy. 2 the humility of Christ (2:5–11). 3 the righteousness of Christ, not our own. 4 peace and contentment.
message: Joy in Christ in all circumstances. “To me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (1:21).

author and date: Paul, from prison, c. AD 60–62.
setting and audience: The church at Colossae, troubled by false teaching.
structure: 1–2 the supremacy of Christ (1:15–20) and warnings against philosophy and ritual. 3–4 the new life and household duties.
message: Christ is the head over all creation and the church, and he is all-sufficient.

author and date: Paul with Silvanus and Timothy, from Corinth, c. AD 50–51. It is among the earliest New Testament writings.
setting and audience: A young church, persecuted and puzzled about those who had died.
structure: 1–3 thanks and Paul’s ministry. 4–5 holiness, the Lord’s return (4:13–18), and being ready.
message: Hope in Christ’s coming; the dead in Christ will rise first.

author and date: Paul, from Corinth, c. AD 51–52.
setting and audience: The same church, with new confusion about the day of the Lord.
structure: 1 judgement and glory. 2 the man of lawlessness and the day of the Lord. 3 work and discipline.
message: Stand firm, for Christ will come. The reading of chapter 2 varies among interpreters.

author and date: Paul, c. AD 62–64, after his first Roman imprisonment. These letters are called the Pastoral Epistles.
setting and audience: Timothy, Paul’s helper, at Ephesus.
structure: 1 false teachers. 2–3 worship and officers (elders and deacons). 4–6 how to minister, and warnings about wealth.
message: The church is “the pillar and buttress of the truth” (3:15). Order serves the gospel.

author and date: Paul, from a Roman prison, c. AD 66–67, near the end of his life.
setting and audience: Timothy, whom Paul charges to hold fast.
structure: 1 do not be ashamed. 2 endure like a soldier. 3 all Scripture is God-breathed (3:16–17). 4 preach the word.
message: Faithfulness to the gospel and to the whole of Scripture. Paul says, “I have fought the good fight” (4:7).

author and date: Paul, c. AD 62–64.
setting and audience: Titus, whom Paul left in Crete to appoint elders.
structure: 1 elders. 2 sound doctrine and the behaviour that fits it. 3 grace and good works (3:4–7).
message: The grace of God teaches us to live well, and our works follow our salvation (3:5).

author and date: Paul, from prison, c. AD 60–62.
setting and audience: Philemon, whose runaway slave Onesimus had become a Christian.
structure: One short letter of 25 verses asking Philemon to receive Onesimus “no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother.”
message: The gospel changes relationships, and Christ’s reconciliation is shown in a master and slave.

author and date: The author is not named (Paul, Barnabas and Apollos have been proposed). It was written before AD 70, since the temple service is in the present tense.
setting and audience: Jewish Christians tempted to go back to the old covenant.
structure: 1–2 the Son is greater than angels. 3–4 greater than Moses, and the rest. 4:14–10:18 the high priest of a better covenant. 10:19–13 faith (ch. 11), endurance and holy living.
message: Christ is better in everything: his sacrifice is once for all (10:10–14), and the new covenant replaces the old. Hebrews contains strong warnings (6; 10) against falling away.

author and date: James, the brother of Jesus and leader of the Jerusalem church, c. AD 45–62.
setting and audience: Jewish Christians scattered abroad.
structure: 1 trials and wisdom. 2 partiality and living faith (2:14–26). 3 the tongue. 4–5 worldliness, patience and prayer.
message: Genuine faith shows itself in works. James agrees with Paul that we are justified by faith alone, and a living faith is never alone.

author and date: The apostle Peter, from “Babylon” (Rome), c. AD 62–64.
setting and audience: Christians scattered through Asia Minor, suffering as exiles.
structure: 1 a living hope and holiness. 2 a chosen people, and submission. 3–4 suffering as Christ did. 5 elders and humility.
message: Christ’s suffering is our example and our salvation, and the glory that follows is our hope.

author and date: Peter, c. AD 65–68, shortly before his death. Some critics doubt Peter’s authorship; the church has accepted it.
setting and audience: The same churches, threatened by false teachers.
structure: 1 grow in knowledge, and Scripture’s reliability (1:20–21). 2 false teachers. 3 the Lord’s return and the new heavens.
message: Hold to the apostolic word, and be ready for the day of the Lord.

author and date: The apostle John, probably from Ephesus, c. AD 85–95.
setting and audience: Churches troubled by false teachers who denied that Christ came in the flesh.
structure: Three tests of true life, woven through the letter: believing the truth about Christ, obeying God, and loving the brothers. The purpose is in 5:13.
message: “That you may know that you have eternal life” (5:13). The letter is a book of assurance.

author and date: John, who calls himself “the elder,” c. AD 85–95.
setting and audience: “The elect lady and her children,” a local church.
structure: One page: walk in truth and love, and do not welcome those who deny that Christ came in the flesh.
message: Truth and love belong together.

author and date: John “the elder,” c. AD 85–95.
setting and audience: Gaius, a faithful friend of the church.
structure: One page: Gaius is praised for his hospitality to travelling teachers, and Diotrephes is rebuked.
message: Support those who go out for the sake of the Name, and walk in the truth.

author and date: Jude, brother of James and of the Lord, c. AD 65–80.
setting and audience: Believers in danger from false teachers.
structure: 1–4 the call to contend for the faith. 5–16 examples of judgement. 17–23 how to persevere. 24–25 the doxology.
message: God is able to keep us from stumbling. Jude uses sources outside the canon (v. 9, 14) and does not make them Scripture.

author and date: John, the apostle, in exile on Patmos, c. AD 95 (traditional) or c. AD 64–68 (some). [INTRA-REFORMED DEBATE]
setting and audience: Seven churches of Asia Minor under pressure from Rome.
structure: 1–3 Christ and the seven churches. 4–5 the throne and the Lamb. 6–19 the seals, trumpets and bowls (read as parallel cycles or as a sequence). 20 the thousand years. 21–22 the new heaven and new earth.
message: Christ the Lamb has won, and all history moves to his return. The main schools of interpretation (idealist, historicist, preterist, futurist) and the three views of the millennium (amillennial, postmillennial, premillennial) are held among the Reformed. [INTRA-REFORMED DEBATE]
